title: Parts of Speech
shortDescription: The eight job-roles every English word plays in a sentence — the map you need before any other grammar topic makes sense.
genZNote: Before you can spot an error, you need to know what job each word is doing. This is the org chart of a sentence.

sections.heading: What is a part of speech?
sections.body: A part of speech is the grammatical role a word plays in a sentence, not a fixed label glued to the word forever. The same word can switch roles: 'water' is a noun in 'drink the water' but a verb in 'water the plants'. Exam questions on parts of speech almost always test this role-in-context, not a memorized dictionary tag.

sections.heading: The eight parts of speech, at a glance

rows: Names a person, place, thing, or idea (Delhi, honesty, table)
Replaces a noun to avoid repetition (he, they, which)
Describes/modifies a noun or pronoun (a tall building)
Shows action or state of being (run, seem, is)
Modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb (ran quickly)
Shows the relationship of a noun/pronoun to another word (on the table)
Joins words, phrases, or clauses (and, but, because)

sections.heading: How to identify a word's part of speech in a sentence
bullets: Look at the word's neighbours, not the word alone — 'light' is a noun ('turn on the light'), adjective ('a light bag'), and verb ('light the candle').
Ask what job it is doing right now: naming something → noun; describing a noun → adjective; showing action → verb.
A word ending in -ly is usually (not always) an adverb — 'friendly' is an exception, it's an adjective.
If it links two clauses, it's a conjunction; if it links a noun to the rest of the sentence via a relationship (in, on, at, by), it's a preposition.

sections.heading: Open class vs closed class
sections.body: Nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs are 'open class' — new words keep entering the language ('to google', 'selfie'). Pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions, and articles are 'closed class' — the list is fixed and small, which is exactly why exams test them heavily: there are only so many prepositions to memorize, so questions can be very specific.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Parts of speech are the eight grammatical roles (noun, pronoun, adjective, verb, adverb, preposition, conjunction, interjection) a word can play depending on context.
keyFacts: The same word can be a different part of speech depending on the sentence — always classify by function, not by memory.
Closed-class words (pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions, articles) are a fixed, small set — high-yield for exams.
Open-class words (nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs) keep growing as language evolves.

highYieldFacts: A word's part of speech is decided by its job in that specific sentence, not a fixed dictionary label.
There are exactly eight traditional parts of speech in English.
commonTraps: Assuming a word is 'always' one part of speech — 'round', 'well', 'light', and 'fast' can each be multiple parts of speech.
Assuming every -ly word is an adverb ('friendly', 'lovely', 'lonely' are adjectives).
mustRemember: Identify part of speech from context first, then apply the rule for that part of speech.
